title: Satyakama, the boy who told the truth about his mother (4.4)
hook: a boy asks his mother who his father was; she doesn't know, and he carries that answer, word for word, to his teacher
tomorrow: the bull, the fire, the swan, the bird

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dog's udgitha, a pack of dogs chanting om, let us eat. Your line was don't chant for food alone. What did you do on purpose instead of on autopilot? Day three hundred thirty-five.
screen: `THE DOG'S UDGITHA — DON'T CHANT FOR FOOD ALONE.`

segments.voice: Name. Date of birth. Father's name. On plenty of old forms, that third line sat near the top, and for some people it was the hardest line on the page. In the Chandogya, a boy who wants to study the Veda faces the spoken version of that line. A teacher will ask: what is your family, your lineage? So the boy, Satyakama, goes home first and asks his mother. What she tells him, and what he does with it, is today's story.
screen: `FATHER'S NAME: ______.` → `WHAT IS YOUR LINEAGE?` → `A BOY ASKS HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: His mother's name is Jabala. She answers him honestly. I don't know your lineage, my son. When I was young, I moved about a great deal working as a servant, and that's when I had you. I don't know. But I am Jabala, and you are Satyakama. So call yourself Satyakama Jabala. Satyakama, son of Jabala. A name made from his mother, not his father. The boy walks to the teacher, Haridrumata Gautama, and asks to become his student. The teacher asks the question. What is your lineage, my dear? And Satyakama repeats his mother's words, all of them, the part that might shame her and the part that might shut him out. I don't know, sir. My mother says she moved about as a servant when she was young, and had me then. She is Jabala, I am Satyakama. I'm Satyakama Jabala. The teacher's reply is the hinge of the story. He says that no one but a true brahmin could speak like that. Fetch the firewood, my dear. I'll take you as a student. You have not gone away from the truth. Look at what counts as the qualification here. Not birth. Not a famous father. The truth, told when a lie would have been easier. His very name holds it: satya means truth, kama means desire. Satyakama, the one who loves truth. Hindus have read this story in different ways. For some, it shows that character is what a brahmin really is. Others, including some traditional commentators, read the teacher as concluding that a boy this truthful must be of brahmin birth after all. Either way, the story keeps the boy at the door, saying I don't know, out loud.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW, MY SON.` · `SATYAKAMA, SON OF JABALA.` · `HE REPEATS IT ALL TO THE TEACHER.` · `YOU HAVE NOT GONE FROM THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `SATYA, TRUTH. KAMA, DESIRE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a quiet truth. Settle into the breath. Think of one true thing about yourself that you usually leave out: something you don't know, something you aren't, a part of your story you skip. You don't have to tell anyone. Just let it be true here, for two minutes, without dressing it up or explaining it away. Breathe with it. Notice whether it feels heavier hidden, or lighter said. The bell holds the time.
Satyakama. The one who loves truth: a boy without a known father, accepted as a student because he told the truth at the door.
Your line: truth is the qualification. Today, when someone asks you something and the easy answer isn't quite true, give the true one, gently. Day three hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Satyakama's story is told to Hindu children as a lesson in honesty, and teachers cite it when discussing whether spiritual standing comes from birth or from character.

original.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, what really is. Satyakāma: one who desires truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a boy who didn't know his father.
what it means: a story about what qualifies someone to learn. not birth. the truth, told when a lie was easier.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 4.4. modern readers often cite it on caste and character; traditional commentators have read the teacher's words in different ways, some broadly, some narrowly.
